title: HEMORRHAGIC DESTRUCTION OF THE BRAIN, SUBEPENDYMAL CALCIFICATION, AND CATARACTS

relationships.phenotype: HEMORRHAGIC DESTRUCTION OF THE BRAIN, SUBEPENDYMAL CALCIFICATION, AND CATARACTS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts (HDBSCC) is caused by homozygous mutation in the JAM3 gene (606871) on chromosome 11q25.

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts (HDBSCC) is caused by homozygous mutation in the JAM3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous mutation in the tight-junction protein JAM3 causes hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts.
checks.explanation: The title states the causal link directly.

checks.claim: The JAM3 gene is located on chromosome 11q25.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygosity mapping identified the disease locus in this family on chromosome 11q25 with a maximum multipoint LOD score of 6.15. Sequence analysis of genes in the candidate interval uncovered a mutation in the canonical splice-donor site of intron 5 of JAM3.
checks.explanation: JAM3 was found among the genes in the 11q25 candidate interval, so it lies on 11q25.

paragraphs.text: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts is a severe autosomal recessive disorder characterized by hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts (Mochida et al. (2010)). Akawi et al. (2013) described a distinctive and catastrophic neonatal presentation, with enlarged ventricles. Affected children have severe neurologic impairment and often die in infancy (Akawi et al. (2013)).

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts is a severe autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Some members of this family had a rare autosomal-recessive syndrome characterized by severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts.
checks.explanation: The paper calls it an autosomal-recessive syndrome with severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain.

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts is characterized by hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: a rare autosomal-recessive syndrome characterized by severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts
checks.explanation: The features match the paper exactly.

checks.claim: Akawi et al. (2013) described a distinctive and catastrophic neonatal presentation of hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: its deficiency leading to a distinctive and catastrophic neonatal presentation of cataracts and hemorrhagic destruction of the brain
checks.explanation: The paper's conclusion states this directly.

checks.claim: Akawi et al. (2013) described enlarged ventricles in the neonatal presentation of hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: Brain MRI at the age of 15 days showed Grade IV intraventricular haemorrhage, severe ventricular dilatation
checks.explanation: Several patients had dilated or enlarged ventricles, and the discussion also mentions large ventricles.

checks.claim: Children affected with hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts have severe neurologic impairment.
checks.evidence_quote: All the affected children in this report had bilateral cataracts and develop progressive neurological impairment, associated with seizures in some individuals.
checks.explanation: The paper also says survivors are severely retarded, with severe spasticity and seizures.

checks.claim: Children affected with hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts often die in infancy.
checks.evidence_quote: The disorder was lethal in 7 out of the 10 cases. Death occurred in the first few weeks of life.
checks.explanation: Most cases ended in death in early infancy.

paragraphs.text: Mochida et al. (2010) described a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates in which several children were affected. They had congenital cataracts, subependymal calcification, and massive intracranial hemorrhage leading to destruction of brain tissue.

checks.claim: Mochida et al. (2010) described a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates in which several children were affected with hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: we identified a homozygous mutation in the tight-junction protein gene JAM3 in a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates. Some members of this family had a rare autosomal-recessive syndrome
checks.explanation: The abstract confirms a large consanguineous UAE family with several affected members. It does not say the affected members were children, and the full text was not supplied.

checks.claim: The affected children in the consanguineous United Arab Emirates family reported by Mochida et al. (2010) had congenital cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: Some members of this family had a rare autosomal-recessive syndrome characterized by severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts.
checks.explanation: Congenital cataracts are stated for the affected family members.

checks.claim: The affected children in the consanguineous United Arab Emirates family reported by Mochida et al. (2010) had subependymal calcification.
checks.evidence_quote: Some members of this family had a rare autosomal-recessive syndrome characterized by severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts.
checks.explanation: Subependymal calcification is stated for the affected family members.

checks.claim: The affected children in the consanguineous United Arab Emirates family reported by Mochida et al. (2010) had massive intracranial hemorrhage leading to destruction of brain tissue.
checks.evidence_quote: However, massive intracranial hemorrhage distinguishes these patients from others.
checks.explanation: The paper reports massive intracranial hemorrhage alongside severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain.

paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) reported additional affected individuals from 3 families with a similar phenotype. Two of the families were consanguineous. These patients further defined the clinical spectrum of the disorder.

checks.claim: Akawi et al. (2013) reported additional individuals from 3 families with a phenotype similar to hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: In this manuscript, we describe three additional novel mutations in JAM3 in patients from different ethnic backgrounds with similar phenotypes
checks.explanation: The paper reports three new families (Turkish, Afghani and Moroccan) with a similar phenotype.

checks.claim: Two of the 3 families reported by Akawi et al. (2013) were consanguineous.
checks.evidence_quote: Consanguinity is evident in two of the families
checks.explanation: Families 1 and 3 were consanguineous; family 2 was not.

checks.claim: The patients reported by Akawi et al. (2013) further defined the clinical spectrum of hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: Some of the other features described in the original family, such as renal anomalies and liver enlargement, were more variable in this patient group.
checks.explanation: The paper compares the new patients with the original family, which broadens the known clinical spectrum.

paragraphs.text: The disorder showed autosomal recessive inheritance in the consanguineous family reported by Mochida et al. (2010).

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts showed autosomal recessive inheritance in the consanguineous family reported by Mochida et al. (2010).
checks.evidence_quote: a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates. Some members of this family had a rare autosomal-recessive syndrome
checks.explanation: The paper describes autosomal recessive inheritance in the consanguineous family.

paragraphs.text: Mochida et al. (2010) used homozygosity mapping in the consanguineous family to map the disorder to chromosome 11q25.

checks.claim: Mochida et al. (2010) used homozygosity mapping in a consanguineous family to map hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts to chromosome 11q25.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygosity mapping identified the disease locus in this family on chromosome 11q25 with a maximum multipoint LOD score of 6.15.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of the consanguineous family, Mochida et al. (2010) found a homozygous mutation in the JAM3 gene, which lies in the 11q25 candidate interval. JAM3 encodes a tight-junction protein that is present in vascular endothelium. The authors suggested that JAM3 is essential for maintaining the integrity of the cerebrovascular endothelium.

checks.claim: Mochida et al. (2010) found a homozygous JAM3 mutation in affected members of the consanguineous family with hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: we identified a homozygous mutation in the tight-junction protein gene JAM3 in a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates.
checks.explanation: The paper reports a homozygous JAM3 mutation in this family.

checks.claim: The JAM3 gene lies in the 11q25 candidate interval for hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: Sequence analysis of genes in the candidate interval uncovered a mutation in the canonical splice-donor site of intron 5 of JAM3.
checks.explanation: JAM3 was among the genes sequenced in the 11q25 candidate interval.

checks.claim: JAM3 encodes a tight-junction protein that is present in vascular endothelium.
checks.evidence_quote: JAM3 is known to be present in vascular endothelium
checks.explanation: Elsewhere the abstract also describes JAM3 as a tight-junction protein gene.

checks.claim: Mochida et al. (2010) suggested that JAM3 is essential for maintaining the integrity of the cerebrovascular endothelium.
checks.evidence_quote: Our results suggest that JAM3 is essential for maintaining the integrity of the cerebrovascular endothelium as well as for normal lens development in humans.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) found further homozygous JAM3 mutations in additional families with the disorder and carried out cellular studies of the mutant proteins.

checks.claim: Akawi et al. (2013) found further homozygous JAM3 mutations in additional families with hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: DNA sequencing revealed three different homozygous missense mutations in JAM3 gene in the three studied families
checks.explanation: Three new homozygous JAM3 mutations were found in three families.

checks.claim: Akawi et al. (2013) carried out cellular studies of the mutant JAM3 proteins.
checks.evidence_quote: we employed confocal fluorescence microscopy to establish their subcellular localization relative to the wild type (WT) JAM3 protein
checks.explanation: The authors carried out cellular localization studies of the p.E116K and p.C219Y mutant proteins.
